war-food-administration.name: War Food Administration
war-food-administration.summary: A US government agency (1943–1945) responsible for producing and distributing food for wartime and civilian needs during World War II, later succeeded by the Farm Service Agency.

frybread.name: Frybread
frybread.summary: A fried flatbread of Native American origin, made from simple ingredients like flour and water, tied to the history of colonial displacement and seen as both a symbol of that and of resilience.

california-roll.name: California roll
california-roll.summary: A type of sushi with crab, avocado and cucumber, usually made rice-side-out; one of the most popular sushi styles in the US, Canada and Australia.

chop-suey.name: Chop suey
chop-suey.summary: A dish of meat and eggs stir-fried with vegetables in a starch-thickened sauce, a staple of American and other overseas Chinese cuisines.

carbonara.name: Carbonara
carbonara.summary: An Italian pasta dish of cured pork, hard cheese, eggs and black pepper, typical of Lazio, which took its modern form and name only in the mid-20th century.

national-council-of-negro-women.name: National Council of Negro Women
national-council-of-negro-women.summary: An American nonprofit founded in 1935 by Mary McLeod Bethune to advance opportunities for African-American women, acting as an umbrella for dozens of affiliate organizations.

lawry-s-the-prime-rib.name: Lawry's Seasoned Salt
lawry-s-the-prime-rib.summary: A seasoned salt blend spun off from the Lawry's restaurant chain by its founders, later growing into a food company now owned by McCormick & Company.

marcel-duchamp.name: Marcel Duchamp
marcel-duchamp.summary: French American artist (1887-1968) who played a key role in developing the avant-garde and became known for anti-art, notably his 1917 urinal piece, Fountain.

francis-picabia.name: Francis Picabia
francis-picabia.summary: French avant-garde painter, writer and typographist (1879–1953) closely tied to Dada, whose shape-shifting style moved through Impressionism, Cubism and later Surrealism.

dada.name: Dada
dada.summary: An international art movement launched in Zürich during World War I, rejecting conventional ideas about art and society; it later influenced Surrealism, pop art and other movements.

frank-lloyd-wright.name: Frank Lloyd Wright
frank-lloyd-wright.summary: American architect (1867–1959) who designed over 1,000 structures across 70 years and pioneered organic architecture and the Prairie School movement, widely called the greatest American architect.

indian-arts-and-crafts-act-of-1990.name: Indian Arts and Crafts Act of 1990
indian-arts-and-crafts-act-of-1990.summary: A 1990 US law barring false marketing of art or crafts as American Indian or Alaska Native made, with fines up to $1 million for violations.
indian-arts-and-crafts-act-of-1990.source_title: Indian Arts and Crafts Act of 1990

george-gershwin.name: George Gershwin
george-gershwin.summary: American composer and pianist (1898–1937) who blended jazz and classical music, writing Rhapsody in Blue, An American in Paris, and the opera Porgy and Bess.

ira-gershwin.name: Ira Gershwin
ira-gershwin.summary: American lyricist (1896–1983) who collaborated with his brother, composer George Gershwin, on classic songs and Broadway shows, continuing to write hits after George's death in 1937.

rhapsody-in-blue.name: Rhapsody in Blue
rhapsody-in-blue.summary: A 1924 composition for piano and jazz band by George Gershwin, blending classical and jazz styles, that helped define the Jazz Age and launched his fame.

an-american-in-paris.name: An American in Paris
an-american-in-paris.summary: A jazz-influenced orchestral tone poem by George Gershwin, first performed in 1928, inspired by the sights and energy of Paris during his time there.

porgy-and-bess.name: Porgy and Bess
porgy-and-bess.summary: An English-language opera by George Gershwin, first performed in 1935, notable for its cast of classically trained African-American singers and songs like 'Summertime.'

albert-frey-architect.name: Albert Frey
albert-frey-architect.summary: Swiss-born architect (1903–1998) who developed the modernist "desert modernism" style centered on Palm Springs, California.

frey-house-ii.name: Frey House II
frey-house-ii.summary: A modernist Palm Springs house designed by architect Albert Frey, completed in 1964 as his own home and noted for its International Style design.

palm-springs-california.name: Palm Springs
palm-springs-california.summary: A desert resort city in California's Coachella Valley, noted for mid-century modern architecture and as a winter destination whose population triples with seasonal visitors, many of them Canadian.

e-stewart-williams.name: E. Stewart Williams
e-stewart-williams.summary: American architect (1909-2005) based in Palm Springs whose mid-century modernist buildings significantly shaped the Coachella Valley's architectural landscape and legacy.

frank-sinatra.name: Frank Sinatra
frank-sinatra.summary: American singer, conductor and actor (1915–1998), nicknamed the "Chairman of the Board," regarded as one of the most influential entertainers of the 20th century.

native-arts-and-cultures-foundation.name: Native Arts and Cultures Foundation
native-arts-and-cultures-foundation.summary: U.S. nonprofit organization that supports Native American, Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian artists and arts organizations through fellowships and project funding.

museum-of-russian-art-minnesota.name: Museum of Russian Art
museum-of-russian-art-minnesota.summary: Nonprofit museum in Minneapolis devoted to Russian art and culture, founded by collectors Raymond and Susan Johnson and opened at its present location in 2005.

house-of-faberg.name: Fabergé
house-of-faberg.summary: A jewellery firm founded in 1842 in Saint Petersburg, famed for the elaborate jewel-encrusted eggs it made for Russian Tsars before the 1917 revolution.

frank-lloyd-wright-building-conservancy.name: Frank Lloyd Wright Building Conservancy
frank-lloyd-wright-building-conservancy.summary: Organization founded in the late 1980s devoted to preserving buildings designed by architect Frank Lloyd Wright and studying his career.

price-tower.name: Price Tower
price-tower.summary: A nineteen-story skyscraper in Bartlesville, Oklahoma, one of the few high-rises designed by Frank Lloyd Wright, completed in 1956 and later named a National Historic Landmark.

marin-county-civic-center.name: Marin County Civic Center
marin-county-civic-center.summary: A government complex in San Rafael, California, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright and built between 1960 and 1976, including an armory, post office and later a jail.

manowar.name: Manowar
manowar.summary: An American heavy metal band formed in 1980 in Auburn, New York, known for fantasy and mythology-themed lyrics, a loud sound, and world records for loudest and longest concerts.

gods-of-war-manowar-album.name: Gods of War
gods-of-war-manowar-album.summary: A 2007 concept album by heavy metal band Manowar centered on the Norse god Odin, meant to be the first in a planned series about war gods from different mythologies.

into-glory-ride.name: Into Glory Ride
into-glory-ride.summary: The second studio album by American heavy metal band Manowar, released in July 1983, bringing themes of fantasy and historical warfare to their music.

sign-of-the-hammer.name: Sign of the Hammer
sign-of-the-hammer.summary: The fourth studio album by the American heavy metal band Manowar, released in October 1984.

selective-service-act-of-1917.name: Selective Service Act of 1917
selective-service-act-of-1917.summary: A 1917 US law authorizing conscription to raise an army for World War I, drafted after the US declared war on Germany and upheld as constitutional by the Supreme Court in 1918.

aleutian-islands-campaign.name: Aleutian Islands campaign
aleutian-islands-campaign.summary: A 1942-1943 World War II campaign fought on Alaska's Aleutian Islands, the only WWII fighting on North American soil, as Japan and US-Canadian forces fought for control of the islands.

battle-of-the-st-lawrence.name: Battle of the St. Lawrence
battle-of-the-st-lawrence.summary: A series of Second World War naval and anti-submarine actions in Canada's St. Lawrence River and Gulf, in which German U-boats sank over 20 ships before Canadian forces disrupted their activity.

rms-lusitania.name: RMS Lusitania
rms-lusitania.summary: A British Cunard ocean liner launched in 1906, briefly the world's largest passenger ship and a Blue Riband holder, sunk by a German U-boat in 1915 with 1,198 lives lost.

woodrow-wilson.name: Woodrow Wilson
woodrow-wilson.summary: The 28th president of the United States, serving 1913 to 1921, the only Democrat to hold the office during the Progressive Era, who led the country through World War I and championed the League of Nations.

henry-luce.name: Henry Luce
henry-luce.summary: American magazine publisher (1898–1967) who founded Time, Life, Fortune and Sports Illustrated, and coined the phrase "American Century" in 1941.

american-century.name: American Century
american-century.summary: A term describing the period since the mid-20th century as dominated by the United States politically, economically, and culturally, coined by publisher Henry Luce in 1941.

four-freedoms.name: Four Freedoms speech
four-freedoms.summary: A January 1941 address by President Franklin D. Roosevelt proposing four fundamental freedoms, marking a break from US non-interventionism before Pearl Harbor.

franklin-d-roosevelt.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
franklin-d-roosevelt.summary: 32nd U.S. president (1933–1945) and the longest-serving in American history, who led the country through the Great Depression and World War II.

winston-churchill.name: Winston Churchill
winston-churchill.summary: British statesman and Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1940 to 1945 and 1951 to 1955, who led Britain through the Second World War.

atlantic-charter.name: Atlantic Charter
atlantic-charter.summary: 1941 joint statement by the United States and United Kingdom setting out postwar goals such as self-determination and disarmament, which became a basis for the United Nations.

triple-entente.name: Triple Entente
triple-entente.summary: An informal alliance built between 1894 and 1907 among Russia, France and Britain, forming a counterweight to the Triple Alliance and fighting together as the Allied Powers in World War I.

richard-irvine-manning-iii.name: Richard Irvine Manning III
richard-irvine-manning-iii.summary: American politician who served as a South Carolina state legislator and as the state's 92nd governor (1859–1931).

greenville-south-carolina.name: Greenville, South Carolina
greenville-south-carolina.summary: A South Carolina city founded in 1797, the state's sixth-most populous with about 70,720 residents in 2020, that grew through cotton mills and rail before shifting toward advanced manufacturing and automotive industries.

spartanburg-south-carolina.name: Spartanburg
spartanburg-south-carolina.summary: A city in South Carolina, the county seat of Spartanburg County, home to several colleges and the corporate headquarters of Denny's.

columbia-south-carolina.name: Columbia, South Carolina
columbia-south-carolina.summary: The capital of South Carolina, founded in 1786 as the state's first planned capital and largely destroyed in an 1865 Civil War fire before being rebuilt.

eugene-o-neill.name: Eugene O'Neill
eugene-o-neill.summary: An American playwright (1888–1953) who brought realist drama techniques to the US and won the 1936 Nobel Prize in Literature plus four Pulitzer Prizes for Drama.

beyond-the-horizon-play.name: Beyond the Horizon
beyond-the-horizon-play.summary: A play by American playwright Eugene O'Neill, his first full-length work to be staged, which won the 1920 Pulitzer Prize for Drama.

anna-christie.name: Anna Christie
anna-christie.summary: A four-act play by Eugene O'Neill that debuted on Broadway in 1921 and won him the 1922 Pulitzer Prize for Drama.

strange-interlude.name: Strange Interlude
strange-interlude.summary: An experimental nine-act play by Eugene O'Neill that won the 1928 Pulitzer Prize for Drama, notable for characters speaking their inner thoughts aloud.

provincetown-players.name: Provincetown Players
provincetown-players.summary: A theater collective founded by George Cram Cook and Susan Glaspell that produced plays in Provincetown and New York from 1915 to 1922, launching Eugene O'Neill's career.

native-american-renaissance.name: Native American Renaissance
native-american-renaissance.summary: Term coined by critic Kenneth Lincoln in a 1983 book for the surge in Native American literary works from the late 1960s onward, following N. Scott Momaday's Pulitzer-winning House Made of Dawn.

house-made-of-dawn.name: House Made of Dawn
house-made-of-dawn.summary: A 1968 novel by Kiowa writer N. Scott Momaday credited with bringing Native American literature into the mainstream, and winner of the 1969 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction.

n-scott-momaday.name: N. Scott Momaday
n-scott-momaday.summary: Kiowa American novelist and poet (1934–2024) whose novel House Made of Dawn won the 1969 Pulitzer Prize and is seen as the first major work of the Native American Renaissance.

joy-harjo.name: Joy Harjo
joy-harjo.summary: American poet, musician and playwright (born 1951) who became the first Native American U.S. Poet Laureate in 2019, serving until 2022, and a leading figure of the Native American literary renaissance.

muscogee-nation.name: Muscogee Nation
muscogee-nation.summary: Federally recognized Native American tribe based in Oklahoma, the largest descendant of the historic Muscogee Confederacy.

tommy-orange.name: Tommy Orange
tommy-orange.summary: American novelist from Oakland, California, whose 2018 debut novel There There was a Pulitzer Prize finalist and won the American Book Award.

louise-erdrich.name: Louise Erdrich
louise-erdrich.summary: Indigenous-American author (born 1954), an enrolled citizen of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa, regarded as one of the leading writers of the Native American Renaissance's second wave.

the-night-watchman-novel.name: The Night Watchman
the-night-watchman-novel.summary: Louise Erdrich's 2020 novel, set on the Turtle Mountain Reservation and inspired by her grandfather's resistance to Indian termination policies; won the 2021 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction.

american-indian-literary-nationalism.name: American Indian literary nationalism
american-indian-literary-nationalism.summary: A late 20th-century intellectual and activist movement holding that Native American literatures should be studied as works of distinct nations rather than as ethnic literature within the American canon.

simon-j-ortiz.name: Simon J. Ortiz
simon-j-ortiz.summary: Native American writer and poet, born 1941 and an enrolled member of the Pueblo of Acoma, seen as a key figure in the Native American Renaissance.

charles-olson.name: Charles Olson
charles-olson.summary: American modernist poet (1910–1970) who linked earlier figures like Ezra Pound to later movements such as the Black Mountain School, and called himself 'an archeologist of morning.'

black-mountain-poets.name: Black Mountain poets
black-mountain-poets.summary: A group of mid-20th-century American avant-garde poets based at Black Mountain College in North Carolina.

black-mountain-college.name: Black Mountain College
black-mountain-college.summary: A private liberal arts college in North Carolina, founded in 1933, whose faculty and students became highly influential in modern art and poetry before it closed in 1957.

american-indian-boarding-schools.name: American Indian boarding schools
american-indian-boarding-schools.summary: Schools established in the U.S. from the mid-17th to early 20th centuries, first by Christian missionaries and later the government, aiming to assimilate Native American children by suppressing their languages and religion.

lynn-riggs.name: Lynn Riggs
lynn-riggs.summary: Cherokee-American author, poet, playwright and screenwriter (1899–1954) whose 1931 play Green Grow the Lilacs was adapted into the musical Oklahoma!

cherokee.name: Cherokee
cherokee.summary: Indigenous people of the Southeastern Woodlands of the United States, historically concentrated in the Carolinas, Georgia, Tennessee and Alabama; by the 19th century settlers classified them as one of the 'Five Civilized Tribes.'

louise-gl-ck.name: Louise Glück
louise-gl-ck.summary: American poet and essayist (1943–2023) whose Nobel Prize in Literature (2020) cited her "unmistakable poetic voice"; she also served as U.S. Poet Laureate from 2003 to 2004.

the-wild-iris.name: The Wild Iris
the-wild-iris.summary: Louise Glück's 1992 poetry collection, which won her the 1993 Pulitzer Prize for Poetry and the Poetry Society of America's William Carlos Williams Award.

studies-in-american-indian-literatures.name: Studies in American Indian Literatures
studies-in-american-indian-literatures.summary: A biannual peer-reviewed academic journal on Native American literature, published by the University of Nebraska Press.

w-azo-a-review.name: Wíčazo Ša Review
w-azo-a-review.summary: Biannual peer-reviewed academic journal of Native American studies, founded in 1985 and published by the University of Minnesota Press.

robert-allen-warrior.name: Robert Warrior
robert-allen-warrior.summary: American Osage scholar and University of Kansas professor, co-author of Like a Hurricane and, with Craig Womack, regarded as a founder of American Indian literary nationalism; served as American Studies Association president, 2016-2017.

craig-womack.name: Craig Womack
craig-womack.summary: Author and professor of Native American literature who wrote Red on Red: Native American Literary Separatism, arguing that Native critics should develop tribal models of criticism rather than Western theory.

neil-armstrong.name: Neil Armstrong
neil-armstrong.summary: American astronaut and commander of Apollo 11, who in 1969 became the first person to walk on the Moon; also a naval aviator and test pilot.

buzz-aldrin.name: Buzz Aldrin
buzz-aldrin.summary: The second person to walk on the Moon, as Lunar Module pilot on Apollo 11 in July 1969, and a former US Air Force fighter pilot.

michael-collins-astronaut.name: Michael Collins
michael-collins-astronaut.summary: An American astronaut (1930–2021) who piloted the Apollo 11 command module in lunar orbit in 1969 while Armstrong and Aldrin made the first Moon landing.

jonas-salk.name: Jonas Salk
jonas-salk.summary: American virologist (1914–1995) who developed one of the first successful polio vaccines, announced in 1955, and chose not to patent it to maximize its global distribution.

eniac.name: ENIAC
eniac.summary: The first programmable, electronic, general-purpose digital computer, completed in 1945 by John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert to compute U.S. Army artillery firing tables; the press called it a 'Giant Brain.'

john-mauchly.name: John Mauchly
john-mauchly.summary: American physicist who, with J. Presper Eckert, designed ENIAC, the first general-purpose electronic digital computer, and helped popularize the stored-program concept in computing.

j-presper-eckert.name: J. Presper Eckert
j-presper-eckert.summary: American electrical engineer (1919–1995) who co-designed ENIAC and the UNIVAC, and invented mercury delay-line memory.

john-bardeen.name: John Bardeen
john-bardeen.summary: American physicist (1908–1991), the only person to win the Nobel Prize in Physics twice, for the transistor and for the theory of superconductivity.

walter-brattain.name: Walter Brattain
walter-brattain.summary: An American physicist (1902–1987) who shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for co-inventing the point-contact transistor, having devoted much of his career to studying surface states.

william-shockley.name: William Shockley
william-shockley.summary: American physicist (1910–1989) who led the Bell Labs team, with John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, that invented the transistor, earning the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.

bell-labs.name: Bell Labs
bell-labs.summary: An American research and development company, formerly part of AT&T, credited with inventing the transistor, the laser and the Unix operating system, among other innovations.

national-institutes-of-health.name: National Institutes of Health
national-institutes-of-health.summary: The main U.S. federal agency for biomedical and public health research, founded in 1887, and one of the funders of the Human Genome Project.

the-watson-institute.name: The Watson Institute
the-watson-institute.summary: An organization for people with special needs in Sewickley, Pennsylvania, founded in 1917 as a children's rehabilitation hospital; in 1952 it was one of the first sites to test Jonas Salk's polio vaccine.

march-of-dimes.name: March of Dimes
march-of-dimes.summary: An American nonprofit founded by President Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1938 to fight polio, later funding Jonas Salk's vaccine before shifting focus to birth defects and premature birth.

pacific-grove-california.name: Pacific Grove, California
pacific-grove-california.summary: A city on Monterey Bay in California, known for its art colony and tourist sites such as Point Pinos Lighthouse.

isabella-abbott.name: Isabella Abbott
isabella-abbott.summary: Hawaiian phycologist and ethnobotanist (1919–2010), the first Native Hawaiian woman to earn a science PhD, who became a leading expert on Pacific marine algae.

nereocystis.name: Nereocystis
nereocystis.summary: A single-species genus of subtidal kelp, also called bull kelp, that forms thick beds on rocks and is an important part of kelp forests.

hanford-site.name: Hanford Engineer Works
hanford-site.summary: A Manhattan Project complex on the Columbia River in Washington state that produced the plutonium used in the Trinity test and the Nagasaki bomb.

gilbert-morgan-smith-medal.name: Gilbert Morgan Smith Medal
gilbert-morgan-smith-medal.summary: An award from the U.S. National Academy of Sciences for excellence in published research on marine or freshwater algae, given every three years since 1979.

herbert-ratner.name: Herbert Ratner
herbert-ratner.summary: American physician (1907–1997), Oak Park's public health director for 25 years, who played a key role in the 1955 polio vaccine controversy.

vaccine-contamination-with-sv40.name: Michele Carbone
vaccine-contamination-with-sv40.summary: A researcher who in 1997 tested decades-old Salk polio vaccine vials and found them contaminated with the SV40 monkey virus.

sv40.name: SV40
sv40.summary: A polyomavirus found in both monkeys and humans that can cause tumors, widely studied as a model virus for eukaryotic DNA replication and transcription.

smoot-hawley-tariff-act.name: Smoot–Hawley Tariff Act
smoot-hawley-tariff-act.summary: A 1930 US law that raised tariffs on over 20,000 imports to protect American industry, but is widely blamed for deepening the Great Depression after trading partners retaliated.

reciprocal-tariff-act.name: Reciprocal Tariff Act
reciprocal-tariff-act.summary: An act enacted in 1934 authorizing the U.S. president to negotiate reciprocal tariff reductions with other nations, reversing the high-tariff policy of the earlier Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act.

america-first-committee.name: America First Committee
america-first-committee.summary: An American isolationist pressure group opposing US entry into World War II, with over 800,000 members at its peak before dissolving in December 1941.

lend-lease.name: Lend-Lease
lend-lease.summary: A US policy of 1941 to 1945 supplying the United Kingdom, Soviet Union, France, China and other Allies with food, oil and materiel worth $50.1 billion, given free as essential to US defense.

dakota-access-pipeline.name: Dakota Access Pipeline
dakota-access-pipeline.summary: A 1,172-mile underground oil pipeline running from North Dakota to Illinois, completed in 2017 after major protests led by the Standing Rock Sioux Reservation.

sioux.name: Sioux (Oceti Sakowin)
sioux.summary: Groups of Native American tribes from the Great Plains, divided into the Dakota and Lakota peoples, together called the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ, or Seven Council Fires.

willard-van-orman-quine.name: Willard Van Orman Quine
willard-van-orman-quine.summary: American logician and philosopher (1908–2000) at Harvard, regarded as one of the most influential philosophers of the 20th century for his work in logic and the philosophy of science.

saul-kripke.name: Saul Kripke
saul-kripke.summary: American philosopher and logician (1940–2022) known for his possible-worlds semantics for modal logic and his 1980 book Naming and Necessity, considered a major 20th-century philosophical work.

analytic-philosophy.name: Analytic philosophy
analytic-philosophy.summary: A broad school of Western philosophy emphasizing rigorous argument, logic and language, contrasted with continental philosophy and dominant since the early 20th century in figures like Frege, Russell and Wittgenstein.

continental-philosophy.name: Continental philosophy
continental-philosophy.summary: A broad group of 20th-century European philosophical traditions, including existentialism, phenomenology and critical theory, usually contrasted with English-speaking analytic philosophy.

american-indian-religious-freedom-act.name: American Indian Religious Freedom Act
american-indian-religious-freedom-act.summary: A 1978 U.S. law restoring religious liberties to American Indians, Alaska Natives and Native Hawaiians, protecting access to sacred sites and traditional ceremonies after such practices had long been banned.

native-american-church.name: Native American Church
native-american-church.summary: Syncretic Native American religion combining traditional beliefs with elements of Christianity and the sacramental use of peyote, originating in Oklahoma Territory in the late 19th century; today the most widespread indigenous religion among Native Americans.

h-l-mencken.name: H. L. Mencken
h-l-mencken.summary: American journalist, essayist and satirist (1880–1956) known for his critical writing on politics, religion and culture, and for his study of American English, The American Language.

friedrich-nietzsche.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
friedrich-nietzsche.summary: A German philosopher and former classical philologist known for critiquing objective truth and Christian morality, who suffered a mental collapse in 1889.

theodore-roosevelt.name: Theodore Roosevelt
theodore-roosevelt.summary: 26th president of the United States (1901–1909), who became president after William McKinley's assassination and, before politics, wrote a history of the Naval War of 1812.

the-philosophy-of-friedrich-nietzsche.name: The Philosophy of Friedrich Nietzsche
the-philosophy-of-friedrich-nietzsche.summary: 1908 book by H. L. Mencken covering both well- and lesser-known parts of Friedrich Nietzsche's life and philosophy, written after Mencken read all of Nietzsche's published works.

susanne-langer.name: Susanne Langer
susanne-langer.summary: American philosopher and writer (1895-1985) known for theories on how art influences the mind, and one of the first American women to hold an academic career in philosophy.

philosophy-in-a-new-key.name: Philosophy in a New Key
philosophy-in-a-new-key.summary: 1941 book by American philosopher Susanne K. Langer arguing that symbolism is the key to understanding how the human mind expresses itself.

van-meter-ames.name: Van Meter Ames
van-meter-ames.summary: American philosophy professor (1898–1985) at the University of Cincinnati who was a founding member of the American Society for Aesthetics and helped draft the congressional bill establishing the National Foundation for the Endowment of the Arts and Humanities.

american-society-for-aesthetics.name: American Society for Aesthetics
american-society-for-aesthetics.summary: An organization founded in 1942 to promote the study of aesthetics, sponsoring conferences and publishing the Journal of Aesthetics and Art Criticism.

morris-weitz.name: Morris Weitz
morris-weitz.summary: American philosopher of aesthetics (1916–1981) who focused on ontology, interpretation, and literary criticism.

arthur-danto.name: Arthur Danto
arthur-danto.summary: An American art critic and philosopher (1924–2013) known for his work in philosophical aesthetics and the philosophy of history.

george-dickie-philosopher.name: George Dickie
george-dickie-philosopher.summary: American philosopher (1926–2020) and professor emeritus at the University of Illinois at Chicago, specialising in aesthetics, philosophy of art and eighteenth-century theories of taste.

art-world.name: Art world
art-world.summary: Everyone involved in producing, presenting, promoting and judging fine art, sometimes used narrowly for the elite level of globalized art.

no-l-carroll.name: Noël Carroll
no-l-carroll.summary: An American philosopher, born 1947, a leading figure in the philosophy of art and film who has taught at the CUNY Graduate Center since 2007.

jerrold-levinson.name: Jerrold Levinson
jerrold-levinson.summary: An American philosopher (born 1948), emeritus professor at the University of Maryland, noted for work on defining art and the aesthetics of music and film.

american-indian-movement.name: American Indian Movement
american-indian-movement.summary: A Native American grassroots movement founded in Minneapolis in 1968 to address discrimination and police brutality, later known for the 1973 Wounded Knee occupation.

ojibwe.name: Ojibwe
ojibwe.summary: An Anishinaabe Indigenous people whose homeland spans the Great Lakes region and northern plains, among the largest Native American and First Nations populations today.

lakota-people.name: Lakota
lakota-people.summary: A Native American people, also called the Teton Sioux, who moved onto the northern Great Plains in the 17th century and made the Black Hills their spiritual center by the 1770s.

wounded-knee-south-dakota.name: Wounded Knee
wounded-knee-south-dakota.summary: A small community on the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation in South Dakota, named for the creek where Sioux chief Crazy Horse's remains were reputedly buried.

ceremonial-pipe.name: Ceremonial pipe
ceremonial-pipe.summary: A type of smoking pipe used by Indigenous peoples of the Americas in sacred ceremonies to offer prayers, mark commitments, or seal treaties.

ho-chunk.name: Ho-Chunk (Winnebago)
ho-chunk.summary: A Siouan-speaking Native American people, also called Winnebago, whose historic territory spanned Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa and Illinois and who were the dominant tribe there before European contact.

kendall-walton.name: Kendall Walton
kendall-walton.summary: American philosopher, born 1939, known for a theory of art as make-believe and for writings on photography, fiction, metaphor and aesthetics.

white-buffalo-calf-woman.name: White Buffalo Calf Woman
white-buffalo-calf-woman.summary: A sacred woman of supernatural origin central to Lakota religion, said to have brought the 'Seven Sacred Rites' to the Lakota people.

sweat-lodge.name: Sweat lodge
sweat-lodge.summary: A domed hut used by Indigenous peoples of the Americas for a purification ceremony of prayer and healing, traditionally led only by knowledgeable Elders.

sun-dance.name: Sun Dance
sun-dance.summary: A Plains Indigenous ceremony in which young men danced for days without food or water as an act of sacrifice; governments in the US and Canada banned it for decades before legal protections later restored it.

orson-welles.name: Orson Welles
orson-welles.summary: American actor and filmmaker (1915 to 1985) considered among the most influential in film history, famed for directing Citizen Kane and the 1938 radio War of the Worlds broadcast that caused public panic.

the-war-of-the-worlds-1938-radio-drama.name: The War of the Worlds (1938 radio drama)
the-war-of-the-worlds-1938-radio-drama.summary: A 1938 Halloween radio episode of The Mercury Theatre on the Air, directed and narrated by Orson Welles as an adaptation of H. G. Wells's novel, notorious for convincing some listeners a real Martian invasion was underway.
the-war-of-the-worlds-1938-radio-drama.source_title: The War of the Worlds (1938 radio drama)

black-elk.name: Black Elk
black-elk.summary: An Oglala Lakota holy man, 1863 to 1950, who fought at Little Bighorn, survived Wounded Knee, and later shared his visions in interviews published as Black Elk Speaks.

oglala.name: Oglala
oglala.summary: One of the seven subtribes of the Lakota people, most of whom now live on the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation in South Dakota.

john-g-neihardt.name: John G. Neihardt
john-g-neihardt.summary: American writer, poet and ethnographer best known for Black Elk Speaks (1932), presented as the Lakota medicine man Black Elk's narrated visions; the book's accuracy remains disputed.

joseph-epes-brown.name: Joseph Epes Brown
joseph-epes-brown.summary: American scholar whose work helped bring the study of Native American religious traditions into higher education, notably his book The Sacred Pipe based on talks with Black Elk.

black-elk-speaks.name: Black Elk Speaks
black-elk-speaks.summary: A 1932 book by poet John G. Neihardt recounting the life and visions of Oglala Lakota medicine man Black Elk, later translated and reprinted worldwide.

scandinavia-house-the-nordic-center-in-a.name: Scandinavia House
scandinavia-house-the-nordic-center-in-a.summary: A cultural center in Manhattan run by the American-Scandinavian Foundation, opened in 2000 to showcase Nordic art, design and performing arts, and to teach Scandinavian languages.
scandinavia-house-the-nordic-center-in-a.source_title: Scandinavia House – The Nordic Center in America

james-polshek.name: James Stewart Polshek
james-polshek.summary: American architect (1930–2022) who founded Polshek Partnership, a New York firm where he was principal design partner for more than four decades.

the-american-scandinavian-foundation.name: American-Scandinavian Foundation
the-american-scandinavian-foundation.summary: An American non-profit promoting cultural exchange between the US and Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden, headquartered at Scandinavia House in New York City.

long-day-s-journey-into-night.name: Long Day's Journey into Night
long-day-s-journey-into-night.summary: An autobiographical play by Eugene O'Neill, written in 1939–1941 and published posthumously in 1956, widely regarded as his finest work.

religious-freedom-restoration-act.name: Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993
religious-freedom-restoration-act.summary: A 1993 US federal law requiring strict scrutiny for laws that burden religious freedom, passed after a Supreme Court ruling had weakened free-exercise protections.

controlled-substances-act.name: Controlled Substances Act
controlled-substances-act.summary: The 1970 U.S. law establishing federal drug policy, creating five drug schedules and empowering agencies like the DEA to regulate manufacture, possession and distribution of substances.

north_america-modern-art-004: Indian Arts and Crafts Act of 1990
north_america-modern-science-007: D.T. Watson Home for Crippled Children
